cards.explanation: The gift Paul singles out is prophecy. Paul, the apostle writing to the church in Corinth, says to pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, “…especially the gift of prophecy.” (1 Corinthians 14:1) He puts it right alongside pursuing love, friends.

The answer is True. The one who speaks in a tongue speaks to God, but the one who prophesies speaks to men. Paul says it's for their edification, encouragement and comfort (1 Corinthians 14:3). Three good things in one sentence, friends, and none of them are small.

The word is himself. Paul says the one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church (1 Corinthians 14:4). One gift builds up the speaker, and the other builds up the whole room. Paul is just laying them side by side, bakers.

The exception is when the speaker interprets. Paul says the one who prophesies is greater, “…unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.” (1 Corinthians 14:5) When the tongue gets interpreted, the whole church can understand it too. Everyone gets a bite, friends.

The word is distinct. Paul asks how anyone will recognize the tune a flute or harp is playing “…unless the notes are distinct?” (1 Corinthians 14:7) If every note melts into the next, you're not hearing a song, you're hearing a mystery. Clear notes let the tune come through, bakers.

The answer is False. Paul asks, “…if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle?” (1 Corinthians 14:8) He's asking who will get ready when the call is muffled. The question points to no one, friends.

Paul's point is that their words must be understood to help. He says, “Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air.” (1 Corinthians 14:9) The flute and the trumpet were his examples, bakers. Words that nobody can understand don't help the people listening.

The word is foreigner. Paul says, “If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me.” (1 Corinthians 14:11) It starts with Paul not knowing the meaning of the speaker's language. After that, the speaker is a foreigner to him right back, friends.

The target is the gifts that build up the church. Paul says, “Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church.” (1 Corinthians 14:12) The Corinthians were already eager, bakers. Paul just points that eagerness at building up the church.

Paul says he will pray with his spirit and his mind, both. He says, “I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind.” (1 Corinthians 14:15) He doesn't pick one or the other, friends, he brings the whole self to prayer. He says the same about singing right after: “I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind.”
The answer is False. Paul says, “I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind.” (1 Corinthians 14:15) Spirit and mind sing together, friends. Nobody gets left in the green room.

The word is Amen. Paul asks how an uninstructed person can say Amen to your thanksgiving when you speak a blessing in spirit. The reason he gives is, “…since he does not know what you are saying?” (1 Corinthians 14:16) Saying Amen means you're agreeing with what was said, bakers, and you can't agree with something you can't follow.

The answer is True, and I love it. Paul says, “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.” (1 Corinthians 14:18) So when he says prophecy comes first in church, it's not because he's never done tongues, friends. He has, more than anybody in the room.

Paul would rather speak five clear words that instruct others. He says, “…in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.” (1 Corinthians 14:19) That math is hard to argue with, bakers. Five words that land are worth more than ten thousand that don't.

The word is evil. Paul says, “In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.” (1 Corinthians 20:14) He tells them to be infants in regard to evil, and mature in their thinking. I think that's a good mix, friends: innocent where it counts, and full-grown in the mind.

The answer is False. Paul says, “Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers. Prophecy, however, is for believers, not for unbelievers.” (1 Corinthians 14:22) So tongues are the sign for unbelievers, not for believers. That statement had half the sentence turned around, bakers.

Paul says they'll say that you are out of your minds. If the whole church speaks in tongues and some uninstructed people or unbelievers come in, “…will they not say that you are out of your minds?” (1 Corinthians 14:23) A visitor who can't understand a word of it isn't going to know what to make of the room, friends.

Paul says the visitor will fall facedown and worship God, and that's quite a turnaround. He says, “…the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God…” (1 Corinthians 14:25) The visitor ends up on his face worshiping, friends. He proclaims that God is truly among them.
